commit.message:
Billing: a recompute after the day tick no longer counts today's 95th-percentile sample twice

dayTick() routes the day, then appends today's transit use to t.hist. Every
compute() after that (any click, the intern, the sales trial) took the last 29
entries of t.hist, which now end on today, and added today's use again: today
counted twice and the 30th day back dropped out. So compute() gave a different
transit bill the second time after each day. p95() now leaves today's sample out
once S.hist says the day has been recorded.

This was the only part of compute() that was not a pure function of S. The rest
of the drift round 1 saw (R right after dayTick vs. a fresh compute) is dayTick
itself changing S after its compute (customers churning, events ending), which
is intended: the next day routes the new state. Scenic circuits' hysteresis is
documented, with a test that two calls converge.

commit.message:
Attacks arrive as on 1.36 again: drop the distributed multi-ingress flood model

Frederic's call for 2.0: keep #153's fixes, NOC breakdown, new vectors, gaming risk
and overlapping attacks, but not the per-port model. It split every flood over each
ingress port with traffic (over a thousand on a big network), stored them all in the
save, routed one pinned flow per port, and with it came the build-order and
victim-scoring bugs found in review.

Each attack is again one entry port at the victim (a.entry): upstream clean-pipe,
Flowspec on the victim's router, IX blackholing, a sacrificial PNI and RouteScript
filter it in that order (ddosMitigation), then scrubbing; what leaks is junk at the
victim spread like its traffic, exactly as on main. Saves from 2.0 builds with
a.entries load: sanitize drops the shares and a 'distributed' entry becomes 'edge'.
Removed: R.ingressPorts, ddosEntries/ddosFold/ddosSlices/ddosCities/ddosHasIx, pinned
flows (and the pinned-rank handling in routing and its reference), the mixed-TCAM
line and the 'across N ports' message, and their tests; the scrubbing source-city
test now uses two victims sharing one center. CHANGELOG #153 bullets describe what
ships and credit #153.

commit.message:
Submarine upgrades that change nothing on a cable can't be bought (#198)

Premium submarine terminals and Optical engineering only extend the
long-haul modes of the coherent optics. On many cable lengths (all of
the Atlantic, and about 17,000-18,500 km like Atlanta to Sydney) neither
changes what any optic carries, yet both could be bought.

subHelps() compares every optic's rate with and without the upgrade,
counting an upgrade that only helps together with the other one. The
link panel disables Install with a note, ACT.subUpgrade refuses, and
the cable order screen disables the toggle and only quotes and charges
picks that still help on the chosen design.

commit.message:
Map: a link's curve only measures the cities that could be in its way

bezGeom() measured every city against every candidate curve, for every link the
first time the map drew it. A curve stays inside the box of its end and control
points, so a city further than the clearance it needs outside that box always
measures as clear; leaving it out gives the same curve. About 4x faster, and
the curves on the big fixture are byte-identical.

commit.message:
Saves get the rules of their mode, whatever their rules say

sanitize() trusted any preset and override in a save, so an edited or imported save
could run a Normal game on puzzle rules (no clock, ever), On-call with infinite money
and open gates, sandbox powers without the sandbox tag, or a scenario off On-call.
Rules now follow the mode: scenarios and the weekly are On-call, a sandbox keeps only
its chaos, a Normal game one of the three Normal presets unchanged.

commit.message:
Requirements: build the possible-diversity map on city indices

The first diversityPossible() call after a save loads (migrate() checks every
customer's requirements) built a graph of every buildable link between all
~28k city pairs, scanning all 475 cable segments for each pair, with string ids
and objects for each of ~19k links: about 0.8 s on a fast machine, ~0.9 s of a
throttled phone's boot. Now the cables come from a table per pair and the graph
holds city indices and one number per risk (each land trench and own cable on
its own; every segment of a cable, or a fabric, sharing one). The answers match
disjointRoutes() over the old link list for all 14,042 sampled pairs, won or not
and with scenario bans.

and a city with nobody to serve only holds a flood its tools soak up. Seeded runs
over a year: no defence or one 1T center cannot win; one 1T center with full
Flowspec and clean pipe wins around day 100 (main needed two centers, day 164).

commit.message:
Regenerate published weekly puzzles when a release's prices break them

--check now re-solves every week not over yet and, when its budget no longer
verifies, regenerates it deterministically: the same puzzle with a new budget
if that works, else a fresh one for the key. A regenerated file carries rev 2,
3...; the game keeps stars per revision, so only that week's stars reset.
Past weeks are left alone unless the game rejects them. release.yml runs it
before the tests on every deploy, weekly-puzzle.yml before making the new
week; either fails only if a week cannot be regenerated.

commit.message:
A carrier's own transit port takes its traffic, with a Carry here switch for other POPs

Transit ports at a POP shared load by free capacity whatever the traffic
was for, so Level Tree's own traffic went out of a Tell-Ya port about
half the time. Traffic bound for a carrier, or for a network that buys
transit from it, now goes out of that carrier's port at the same POP
first (the shorter AS path). Each such port is still an ordinary transit
exit, so POPs without one use it when nothing nearer has room.

A new switch on each transit port, Carry here, pulls that traffic from
every POP across your network to this port. The default, Nearest port,
keeps using the closest transit port from POPs that have no port of the
carrier. The switch only shows when another carrier's port could take
the traffic instead.

Prefer-marked ports, Backup only, RouteScript and Auto-TE keep their say,
and any Prefer-marked transit port switches the rule off. Traceroute
follows the same rule and says why it picked an exit. The setting is
repaired in sanitize(); old saves load with it off.

The routing reference test now has several carriers sharing POPs, ports
that carry, backup ports and RouteScript, and its reference loop knows
the new ranks.

commit.message:
Backbone technology: plain IGP, LDP, RSVP-TE, SR-MPLS, SRv6; two new RSVP-TE routers

Each router is classed by the highest backbone it runs and has a vendor. Upgrades
are paid one step at a time and any level paid for can run. Higher levels use
less router CPU, label switching makes pass-through traffic cheaper, Auto-TE and
RouteScript need RSVP-TE or above, and POPs whose routers can't run the backbone
stay outside it. Mixed vendors at the top of what their routers can do get
interop failures. Saves with Auto-TE keep the old rules; puzzles, Architect and
scenarios are unaffected.

Restore what the merge from main dropped from the carrier's own transit port

The merge kept main's version of compute(), the link actions and panels, the
traceroute exit list and the CHANGELOG, so the city panel called a carryCtl()
that no longer existed and routing never ranked a carrier's own port. Put the
ranking back into compute() on top of the current rank lists and island split,
along with setCarry, carryCtl, the traceroute carry flag, the reference loop in
the routing test and the CHANGELOG bullet. Drop a stale label main had removed
and sort the dictionaries.

The tests follow main too: saves are read from their slot, RouteScript needs
the core to run, Not That Telecom stands in for Cogentle (whose share is now
small), and the flood test uses a smaller sacrificial PNI and IX flood because
a carrier's own traffic now takes its share of the one transit port first.

The intern's PNI order counts the traffic the PNI list shows (#244)

It now uses pniVal(net,city).want: what your users there send over transit, an exchange or a PNI elsewhere, from live routing.

commit.message:
Prefer keeps the say at its own POP only, and the direct ranks stop slowing the game day

Review of #205:

- Prefer no longer switches the carrier-direct rule off for the whole network.
  A POP with a Prefer-marked transit port keeps what Prefer says; every other
  POP keeps the rule. compute(), traceroute and the reference loop in the tests
  all use the same per-POP rule, and a new test covers it (New York and Chicago,
  Prefer on one POP's Tell-Ya port).
- dayTick() cost. The harness is neutral (the same page on both sides differs by
  1%), but the cost was real: the four extra rank passes inside compute()'s main
  loop made V8 deoptimise compute() 954 times in 30 game days against 46 on main.
  The direct ranks now run in a small function of their own, in the plain way the
  reference loop does (their lists are one carrier's ports), so the main loop is
  the one main has, and the setup moved out of compute(). 61 deopts instead of 954.
- Italian: "Porta qui" read as "port here" next to "Porta più vicina"; it is
  "Instrada qui" now, and "Ogni POP instrada il traffico..." matches.
- Help text: says that real BGP carries the traffic from every POP (the shorter
  AS path beats IGP distance), that Carry here does that here, and that Nearest
  port is the default. All six languages.

commit.message:
A plug-in optic too short for a subsea cable is no longer sent to upgrades that cannot stretch it (closes #253)

On an own subsea cable, the hint under an optic that cannot reach the route
said "Consider submarine terminals or optical engineering" for every optic.
Those upgrades only lengthen the Sienna WaveMagic 1.6T and 3.2T transponder
modes (optModes()); the 400ZR+ and 800ZR+ plug-ins gain nothing, also with
both upgrades in service. Perth to Cape Town (8,891 km) showed it: 800ZR+
reaches 5,400 km and the advice was to buy $17M of upgrades that change
nothing.

chWhy() now asks whether the optic would reach with both upgrades in service
(withSubUps()). If so, the advice stays. If not, the hint says the upgrades do
not stretch this optic and names the optics that do reach the route. A
consortium seat and a leased line keep their own message.

commit.message:
Prototype: route each game day in a Web Worker built from the page's own script

The day is split around its routing (dayPre, compute, dayPost). In play, S goes to a
worker started from a Blob URL of the page's inline game script (nothing fetched), the
day waits for R and finishes when it arrives. Actions, failures, events and the intern
still route synchronously; an action mid-day wins over the worker's stale answer.
R crosses as plain data: R.ef as its raw arrays (transferred), flows as columns.
Tests and any worker failure keep the synchronous path.

commit.message:
Routing keeps its structural tables between calls and runs its hot loops as small functions, identical results

compute() was one 33 KB function that V8 never kept optimised: it ran in baseline code, boxing every number,
and was recompiled in the background (about a second of compile each time on a loaded machine) only to deopt.
Its stages now run as closures of their own (compute's own bytecode: 7.7 KB) and the money is computeMoney().
The shortest paths and the exit lists (okBy, reach, BRJ/LIST, DSEL) are kept between calls under keys built
from everything they depend on (29-route-cache.js). Exits and paths have one object shape each.
The equivalence tests compare cached against uncached routing; tests/route-cache.test.js checks the keys.

commit.message:
Routing adds up per-kind traffic in typed arrays and keeps its group array's storage: half the allocation per compute

R.egT and R.netEg were summed by key in push(), which boxes every new value; they are now Float64Array sums written
back after routing, in the same order and key order. The first group G was emptied with length=0 for every flow,
which gives back its storage so the next push allocates it again; it is now G[0..GN). 27.5 MB -> 13.5 MB per compute.

files.patch:
@@ -0,0 +1,77 @@
+---
+name: gameplay-rules
+description: The design rules of Series of Tubes, each with an id and the test that enforces it. Use whenever you add or change cities, countries, networks (NETS, upstreams, traffic shares, presence), cables, exchanges, data centers, customers, scenarios, puzzles, presets or rules, balance numbers or progression, and before committing any such change.
+---
+
+# Gameplay rules
+
+These are what the game promises, held up by `tests/gameplay-rules.test.js` (one `test()` per id, on the live
+`CITIES`, `NETS`, `CABLES`, `SCN`, `PZ`, `PRESETS`…). Each rule is true of the intended design.
+
+## Procedure
+
+1. Changing anything above? Run `npm test -- tests/gameplay-rules.test.js` (under a minute) before committing.
+2. A failure names what breaks the rule and how to fix it. Fix the data or the code.
+3. Only when real life really is different, add an entry to `EXCEPTIONS` in the test (keyed by rule id, sorted, with
+   its reason in plain words). Never delete or loosen a check to make it pass. A stale exception fails too.
+4. A new rule gets an id in the right section here, one line, a why, and its own `test('ID: …')`.
+
+## World
+
+| Id | Rule | Why |
+| --- | --- | --- |
+| W1 | Every city has a country code (`cc`, ISO 3166-1 alpha-2; territories have their own: PR, GU, RE, MQ, CW…), a region, a landmass and coordinates. | Borders, prices and the eyeball rule all hang off the country. |
+| W2 | Every country on the map has at least two consumer networks of its own: an eyeball network, or a Tier 1 or Tier 2 incumbent that sells to homes, whose home markets (`cc` on the network) include that country and which has a PoP there. | Real countries have competing local ISPs, and peering locally is half the game. Add real operators in `src/game/30-networks/32-homegrown-eyeballs.js`. |
+| W3 | Every city can buy transit from someone, or is a documented exception (Pitcairn: land your own cable; Stuttgart: peering only). | A start or an expansion must never be a dead end by accident. |
+| W4 | Cable pairs join two distinct real cities, have a length, and cable ids are unique. | Broken landings break routing and the own-cable planner. |
+| W5 | A city alone on its landmass has a cable or a beach to land one. | Islands are reachable. |
+
+## Networks
+
+| Id | Rule | Why |
+| --- | --- | --- |
+| N1 | Network ids and ASNs are unique; ASNs are public (the real one for real-world networks). | Saves key on ids; players look ASNs up. |
+| N2 | Names are puns: no network, cable, exchange, data center, router, optic, cable ship or maintenance club is called by a real name (blocklist `REAL_NAMES` in the test), and no lazy "-ish" names. | CLAUDE.md. Add the real name to the blocklist whenever you add its pun. |
+| N3 | Every non-Tier-1, non-content network is in a founding Tier 1's customer cone (`up`), or is a documented island (transit-free incumbents, China, Korea, Australia…). Upstreams exist and are never content. | Tier 1 by customer cone (#85): a new network outside the cones makes Tier 1 harder for every save, old ones included. |
+| N4 | No upstream cycles. | Cones must be trees, not loops. |
+| N5 | Traffic shares are positive and below 20%; `NSH` and the regional tables sum to 1; content carries at least 30%. | Shares drive every flow; eyeballs mostly ask for traffic. |
+| N6 | Every network has a type, a peering policy (selective ones state `minIx`/`minPni`), a colour and a translated blurb; carriers have a price. | Panels and the peering rules read them. |
+| N7 | PoPs are real, distinct cities; exchange ports only where the city has an exchange and the network has a PoP. | Presence follows PeeringDB-style reality. |
+
+## Modes and rules
+
+| Id | Rule | Why |
+| --- | --- | --- |
+| M1 | On-call is the classic game: it equals `RULE_DEF`, and a save without rules loads as On-call. The seeded suites (`tests/game.test.js`, `tests/rules.test.js`) are its behaviour. | Old saves never change under them. |
+| M2 | Presets are ordered: Change Freeze never harsher than On-call, BGP at 3 a.m. never gentler (chaos, lead times, market; and a seeded year of incidents). | The names promise it. |
+| M3 | Every subsystem that can annoy the player reads a rule: outages and events (`chaos`), DDoS, sold-out routes, de-peering and hardware prices (`market`), lead times (`lead`), the clock. A quiet ruleset gives a quiet year. | Rules are presets of flags, not separate code. |
+| M4 | Scenarios and the weekly challenge always run On-call plus their own `S.scn.rules`. | Fair scores. |

+name: Weekly puzzle
+
+# Every Sunday morning: make this week's puzzle (scripts/weekly-puzzle.js), scenario (scripts/weekly-scenario.js) and
+# Architect run (scripts/weekly-architect.js),
+# commit them to main as a data-only change, and redeploy the live release with them, once. Weeks start Sunday
+# 06:00 Berlin time; 03:37 UTC is 04:37 in winter and 05:37 in summer, so the files are live before the week starts.
+#
+# No version bump, so no release: auto-release.yml only runs when package.json changes (and pushes made with
+# the workflow token start no workflows at all). The deploy itself is release.yml, still the only workflow
+# that can write to Pages, started from the live release's tag with weekly=true: it rebuilds exactly that
+# release with every weekly puzzle from main added, in the same "pages" concurrency group as any release.
+on:
+  schedule:
+    - cron: '37 3 * * 0'
+  workflow_dispatch:
+    inputs:
+      key:
+        description: Week to make, e.g. 2026-W45 (default the week starting this Sunday)
+        required: false
+      deploy:
+        description: Redeploy the live release with it
+        type: boolean
+        default: true
+
+permissions:
+  contents: write   # commit the puzzle to main
+  actions: write    # start release.yml
+
+concurrency:
+  group: weekly-puzzle
+  cancel-in-progress: false
+
+jobs:
+  puzzle:
+    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
+    timeout-minutes: 30
+    env:
+      GH_TOKEN: ${{ github.token }}
+      KEY: ${{ inputs.key }}
+    steps:
+      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
+        with:
+          ref: main
+      - uses: actions/setup-node@v7
+        with:
+          node-version: 24
+          cache: npm
+      - run: npm ci
+      # Weeks already out that main's prices no longer fit are regenerated first, so the new week's history is current.
+      - name: Fit the published weeks to main
+        run: node scripts/weekly-puzzle.js --check && node scripts/weekly-scenario.js --check && node scripts/weekly-architect.js --check
+      - name: Make the puzzle and the scenario
+        run: |
+          set -euo pipefail
+          if [ -n "$KEY" ]; then
+            [[ "$KEY" =~ ^[0-9]{4}-W[0-9]{2}$ ]] || { echo "::error::$KEY is not a week key"; exit 1; }
+            node scripts/weekly-puzzle.js --key "$KEY"
+            node scripts/weekly-scenario.js --key "$KEY"
+            node scripts/weekly-architect.js --key "$KEY"
+          else
+            node scripts/weekly-puzzle.js
+            node scripts/weekly-scenario.js
+            node scripts/weekly-architect.js
+          fi
+      - name: Check every weekly puzzle
+        run: node scripts/weekly-puzzle.js --check && node scripts/weekly-scenario.js --check && node scripts/weekly-architect.js --check && npm test -- tests/weekly-puzzle.test.js tests/puzzles.test.js tests/weekly-scenario.test.js tests/weekly-architect.test.js
+      - name: Commit it to main
+        run: |
+          set -euo pipefail
+          git add site/puzzles/weekly site/scenarios/weekly site/architect/weekly
+          # Data only: anything else changed means something is wrong.
+          if git status --porcelain | grep -v -e ' site/puzzles/weekly/' -e ' site/scenarios/weekly/' -e ' site/architect/weekly/' | grep -q .; then git status --porcelain; echo "::error::unexpected changes"; exit 1; fi
+          if git diff --cached --quiet; then echo "Nothing new to commit."; exit 0; fi
+          git -c user.name="github-actions[bot]" -c user.email="41898282+github-actions[bot]@users.noreply.github.com" \
+            commit -m "Weekly puzzle and scenario $(git diff --cached --name-only | grep -o '[0-9]\{4\}-W[0-9]\{2\}' | sort -u | paste -sd ' ')"
+          git push origin HEAD:main
+      - name: Redeploy the live release with it
+        if: github.event_name == 'schedule' || inputs.deploy
+        run: |
+          set -euo pipefail
+          tag=$(gh release list --repo "$GITHUB_REPOSITORY" --exclude-pre-releases --exclude-drafts --limit 1 --json tagName -q '.[0].tagName')
+          [ -n "$tag" ] || { echo "::error::no release to redeploy"; exit 1; }
+          # Releases from before the weekly puzzles cannot take them (and their game would not read them).
+          if ! git fetch --no-tags --depth=1 origin "refs/tags/$tag" || ! git show FETCH_HEAD:.github/workflows/release.yml | grep -q '^      weekly:'; then
+            echo "::notice::$tag predates weekly puzzles; the puzzle is on main and ships with the next release."; exit 0
+          fi
+          gh workflow run release.yml --repo "$GITHUB_REPOSITORY" --ref "$tag" -f tag="$tag" -f weekly=true
+          echo "Redeploying $tag with the weekly puzzles."

+## [2.1.0] — 2026-10-31
+
+- Your backbone now runs a technology you choose: plain IGP, LDP/MPLS, RSVP-TE, SR-MPLS or SRv6. Each step up costs plenty and uses less router CPU: label switching makes traffic that only passes through a POP cheaper for its router, and Auto-TE and RouteScript now need RSVP-TE or higher. Routers only run what they support, so a POP with an older router stays outside the backbone, and mixing vendors at the very top of what their routers can do brings interop failures. Networks that already have Auto-TE keep it exactly as it is.
+- An upgraded backbone brings new customers: L3VPNs for enterprises from LDP/MPLS, flex-algo low-latency links from SR-MPLS and network slices from SRv6.
+- A seat on a consortium cable can be lit with the optics you have: add regen sites in the landing stations along the cable. Before, a seat bought at level 2 or 3 stayed dark until long-haul transponders arrived at level 4.
+- List spare capacity with a capacity broker as a standing listing: pick how many alien waves (or your spare pair) to sell, and the broker sells them off over time as carriers on that route want capacity. Each route's market is sized by the eyeballs at both ends, and a busy route sells in days while a road to nowhere sells maybe once, so renting out long empty fibers is no longer a money machine (#203).
+- Two new routers for RSVP-TE backbones: the refurbished Brocadabra MLX-16 with 400G ports, and the Extremely Networks SLX 9740 with 1.6T ports.
+- From RSVP-TE up, fast reroute has backup paths ready, so customers lose only half as much happiness while a link is cut.
+- An interop lab in the NOC tests your vendors against each other first and cuts interop incidents by 60%.
+- Four new badges for your backbone: Label switcher, Bleeding edge, Single-vendor shop and Vendor zoo.
+- The chaos monkey's notice in the NOC no longer has an Open button that did nothing; the monkey's own card is right above it (#226).
+- The puzzle list counts each section's own stars: architect runs show theirs next to their title, and the pack total now sits right above the packs, the stars that unlock the next one (#231).
+- The intern's notes now name the exchanges it peered at: a city's first exchange showed as the city, so "Apfelwein-IX, London" really meant Apfelwein-IX and LYNX (#228).
+- Cancelling an IRU, giving up your own fiber or decommissioning a POP now puts the optics on its fibers back on the spares shelf, instead of throwing them away (#229).
+- Big networks freeze for less on every game day and every click: working out where traffic goes skips exits whose route is already full, so a game day takes about 40% less time (#210). Traffic goes exactly where it went before.
+- Premium submarine terminals and Optical engineering can no longer be bought on a cable where they would change nothing (#198). The button now says so, and an upgrade that only helps together with the other one stays available.
+- A wave size that is sold out on a route can no longer be reached by upgrading a smaller wave on it (#201). The upgrade button says how long it is sold out, just like when buying.
+- Choosing Both for a PNI with one member now really splits it: the second member arrives in the other building when the augment lands, instead of joining the first (#219).
+- The Open button next to your intern's weekly shift report in the NOC now opens the Standing orders sheet, where the whole week is laid out (#226). Before, it did nothing.

+## [2.0.0] — 2026-10-30
+
+**Series of Tubes 2.0: one game, four doors.** Some of you wanted a calmer game, some a harder one, some a quick puzzle over coffee and some a playground where nothing can go wrong. So now every network starts behind a door, and the rules you pick stay with that network for good. Your saved games carry on exactly as they were.
+
+**Normal** comes in three flavours. Change Freeze is the calm one: a third of the outages, no DDoS floods, and deliveries in days instead of months. On-call is the game you know. BGP at 3 a.m. is for people whose pager is a personality: more outages, longer ones, more attacks, and fiery badges to prove you survived. In your first month you also pick a charter: a global backbone, or a low-latency boutique racing the speed of light.
+
+**Sandbox** is a real sandbox now: everything unlocked from day one, money that never runs out, and a chaos dial from nothing ever breaks to spicy.
+
+**Puzzles** are small networks that carry real traffic, routed exactly like the big game. Deliver every flow for the first star, stay on budget for the second, and survive any single cut for the third. When your build earns a star, the chaos monkey runs round the map snipping every trench and cable to prove it. A new puzzle arrives every Sunday morning, the same for everyone.
+
+**Architect runs** grow one network brief by brief. New sites sign up, some become mission-critical, a city closes, traffic outgrows its tubes, and the chaos monkey reviews every brief before the next customer signs. Three handmade runs to start, and a fresh one every Sunday with its HQ somewhere new.
+
+**Scenarios** are themed crises against the clock: a cut cable, a peering spat, a flood week, a race for low latency. A new one comes out every Sunday too.
+
+And in On-call and BGP at 3 a.m., a **chaos monkey** sometimes moves into your network for a few months and snips tubes on purpose, the ones without a backup path first. Outlast it without a customer noticing and it pays; throw it a banana if you have had enough.
+
+**Also new:** Tier 1 works like the real thing, so peering with the big club brings their customers along. A NOC intern carries out your standing orders. Customers call when your network can serve them, not only when your level says so. You can buy a seat on a consortium subsea cable, see at a glance whether a PNI is worth it, keep several networks and play two side by side, and every router model has its own face.
+
+### One game, four doors
+
+- A new start screen with four doors: Puzzles, Sandbox, Normal, and Scenarios & weekly. Every network now picks its rules when it starts, and they stay locked for that network; your saved games carry on exactly as before.
+- Normal comes in three flavours. Change Freeze has a third of the outages and no DDoS floods, delivers PNIs, cross-connects and builds in days instead of months (#151), and skips hardware shortages, sold-out routes and de-peering at exchanges. On-call is the classic game. BGP at 3 a.m. brings almost twice the outages, lasting half as long again, and twice the DDoS. The HUD and the share card show which one you picked.
+- Sandbox is a real sandbox now (#188): everything is unlocked from day one, your own subsea cable included, money never runs out, deliveries are quick, and you pick how much chaos you want, from none to spicy.
+- Pick a charter in your first month of a Normal game: Global backbone (the game as you know it, and the default) or Low-latency boutique (#187). The boutique gets more trading firms, pays them 40% more and has its own win, Speed of Light: beat the fastest leased latency on three finance routes with your own glass while two latency customers pay you. It comes with a badge and shows on your share card.
+- Badges now come in variants: games under the Change Freeze rules earn frosted Freeze-dried badges, and games under BGP at 3 a.m. earn fiery ones worth bragging about. Earning a badge under harder rules than before upgrades it in your collection on this device, and the badge list counts how many of each kind you have. On-call games earn the standard badges; Sandbox and puzzles earn none.
+- Keep several networks on one device, and play two of them side by side in two browser windows. The title screen lists your networks, newest first, with their day, tier, cash and when you last played; tap one to continue it, or use ⋯ to export or delete it. Starting a scenario, the weekly challenge or a new network, or importing a save, now adds a network instead of replacing the one you have, and you can rename a network from the menu. Each window remembers its own network when you reload it. If a network is already open in another window, you can switch to it or take it over, and the other window steps aside instead of both saving over each other. Your existing save carries on as your first network.
+- A tidier start screen: language first, then your network's name, the doors, three compact difficulty buttons with the chosen one explained below, and one drop-down for your home city with the five suggested homes at the top.
+- Pick your own AS number next to your network's name when you start (#135). Leave it empty and the game picks one, and the round green arrow in the name box suggests another name.
+
+### Puzzles
+
+- Puzzles: small networks that carry real traffic, routed exactly like the main game (#190). Each puzzle has flows to deliver (eyeballs pulling from a content origin, circuits between two cities with a latency cap, best-effort traffic that may drop), and the map shows every link's load as it fills. Earn up to three stars: everything delivered, under budget, and still delivered when any single trench or cable is cut. Build with the real tools: link sizes from 10G to 800G, parallel links in the same trench or on a diverse route (also from the link panel), routers with real ports and limits, routing metrics, standby, lowest-latency paths for circuits, and the redundancy check. The whole world is open: any city can get a POP if it helps. Parallel links show their count and sizes, and selecting a city lights up every path it has. Eighteen puzzles in five packs, each teaching one idea: Fat Pipes, Router Rodeo, Traffic Cops, N-1 Club and Grand Tour. No clock, no bills, nothing breaks, and your main game is never touched.
+- A new weekly puzzle every Sunday morning, the same for everyone: a themed puzzle with its own traffic, such as an ocean crossing, a ring, a latency sprint, island hopping or a detour around a busy hub, with its own name and a budget tuned so three stars take a smart design. The Puzzles door says "New this Sunday!" until you have played it, the list counts down to the next one, and your streak and share line use the week's name. A new puzzle week starts on Sunday at 06:00 Berlin time; offline, the game still has a weekly puzzle of its own.
+- Every puzzle now has the chaos monkey: when your build earns a new star, it runs round the map snipping each trench and cable in turn, and the cities that lose traffic say how much. Let it loose again whenever you like, or skip straight to the stars.
+- In puzzles, the map now shows whether the tubes between two cities share one trench or take separate paths, at any zoom: one trench is drawn as a bundle with a "2× one trench" tag, separate paths bow apart with a "2 paths" tag.
+- When a new release changes prices so that this week's or a coming week's puzzle no longer adds up, that puzzle gets a fair new budget, and only its stars start again. Weeks that are over keep theirs.
+
+### Architect runs
+
+- Architect runs, under Puzzles: grow one network brief by brief, from a single tube to a ring that shrugs off any cut. Your build carries over between briefs, mission-critical sites must survive any single trench or cable cut with room on the detour, and a chaos monkey runs round the map snipping tubes before the next customer signs. Three runs to start: Euro Run, Coast to Coast and Pacific Rim.
+- A new Architect run every week: every Sunday a fresh HQ somewhere in the world and six or seven briefs, each built around the network you already have, with its own stars. Sites can outgrow their tubes, so some briefs are about making room. Later briefs stay a surprise in every Architect run: their cities only appear when they come.
+
+### Scenarios
+
+- A new weekly scenario every Sunday morning too, the same for everyone: a themed crisis such as a cut cable, a peering spat, a big event, a flood week, island hopping, a race for low latency, a push across a continent or a shoestring budget, in about a year of game days. It sits at the top of Scenarios & weekly with a countdown and a "New this Sunday!" badge, has its own goal and progress card, a par to beat, a weekly streak and a result line to share. Offline, the classic weekly challenge stands in.
+- Scenario tuning: every handmade scenario now asks for what its story is about, with shorter clocks where it was won in a tenth of the time. Mind the Gap, Cape to Cairo and Order and Progress count cities and IX.brrr ports only when your network joins them up; Fibre to the Basement also wants 500 Gbps served; in Anchors Away nobody sells transit in Tallinn and ships really do drag their anchors over the Baltic links, while the Great Firewall's losses no longer break your 99.5% streak; in the Cogentle Spat, Goggle wants a lot more of your traffic before it peers; Flood Season's terabit floods count when your scrubbing or Flowspec took them; Stepping Stones and Mid-Atlantic Accent start with 5M, enough to light the whole 1.6T chain. Gangnam Style Peering is now really about sender pays: Seoul transit carries a fee on every Gbps, the three incumbents only peer over a paid PNI, and Korean users notice every millisecond, so you win by hauling cheap Tokyo transit while keeping Seoul fast and in profit.
+
+### The chaos monkey
+
+- A chaos monkey now and then moves into your network in On-call and BGP at 3 a.m., and snips a tube every couple of weeks for 120 to 240 days, tubes with no backup path first. Its snips replace the usual random outages while it is here; get through the visit without a customer noticing for a resilience bonus and a new badge, or throw it a banana to send it home early. The "Met the Backhoe" badge is now "Met the Chaos Monkey", earned on its first visit; badges you already have stay yours.
+
+### Build your network your way
+
+- Customers now call when your network can already serve them, not only when your level says so (#187). A fast path between two finance cities brings trading firms, lit dark fiber brings AI interconnects, two diverse paths in one country bring sovereign clouds and broadband in a big city brings cloud gaming, each at its smallest size and with a note on what they spotted; your level still makes them bigger and more frequent.
+- Routers, line systems and optics one level above yours can be had early as a vendor demo unit (#187). Ask the vendor, wait about two weeks, then pay 60% over list until your level catches up; and you can dig your own dark fiber from level 2 as a pioneer, at 60% more than the level 3 price.
+- Take a seat on a new consortium subsea cable (#173). Capacity conferences offer them, and now and then a consortium calls from level 2: pay your share of the build, wait for the ship, then own one, two or four fiber pairs and light them with your own optics, your way onto your own subsea glass before Tier 1. A cut on that cable cuts your pairs too.
+- Hire a NOC intern and give them standing orders: from customer level 2, Kevin from the night shift, Anycast Annie or Tracy Route runs your rules once a game day and pays exactly what your own clicks would. Keep transit above a multiple of its peak, add or swap routers above a load, take free caches, peer at every IX and PNI with the big networks every week, sign ready customers and decline tiny ones, rush repairs, light more fiber and retire small parallel waves. Each order has a pause switch, its own settings, a monthly budget and per-POP exceptions, never breaks a customer's or a bank's transit requirement, and shows what it adds to your monthly bill. The Ops sheet opens with the intern's mood and a weekly shift report, which is also the one notice a week the intern leaves in the NOC (#98, #100, #102, #181, #185, #192, #177).
+- The intern only signs a customer after a trial run shows the network can carry them without hurting anyone else, and rushes every repair that has a price, while the budget lasts (#185). The bulk peering and PNI batches live in the Ops sheet, next to the orders that repeat them (#181, #192).
+- Open a new city from a template in one tap: POP, broadband, transit, an IX port and the redundancy kit, priced up front, with your standing orders taking it from there (#98, #192).
+- Utilities join route servers and request eligible peers across every joined IX, install missing PoP redundancy hardware and balance caches between sites, and request a cache from each eligible provider at each site. A POP's Infra tab shows the redundancy kit as one line with its price, above the rows it fills in.

+- Every router model has its own picture: open one of your POPs and its router sits next to the city's name.
+
+### Peering and Tier 1
+
+- Tier 1 now works like the real thing: peer with the Tier 1 club and their customers come along for free (#85). A PNI or an exchange session reaches the networks you peer with and everyone who buys transit from them, so you no longer chase every tiny ISP for the win; only networks that buy transit from nobody, like the content giants and the big incumbents, still need peering of their own. Small networks and more real eyeball ISPs now buy transit from real-world upstreams, a peer's customers are tried after your direct peers and before transit (so peering widely still pays), the traceroute shows the hand-off, and the Road to Tier 1 card counts who already comes along. Games already won stay won.
+- The peering inbox is gone: your peering policy now answers every peering request for you. Open accepts everyone, Selective accepts small networks on the exchange and newcomers with an up-to-date PeeringDB and quietly declines the rest, and Closed declines them all; once a week the NOC log sums it up, like "Peering desk: 7 new sessions at DE-KICKS and HAMS-IX, 3 declined (Selective)". +- Palau's and the Marshall Islands' main networks now show their real AS numbers instead of ones borrowed from networks elsewhere.

+### Prices, routing and money
+
+- Prices now follow how connected each city really is, based on public peering and routing data. Every city on the map now has it, from Düsseldorf and Riga to Malé, the Caribbean and the Russian Arctic. Transit costs up to 1.8× more in cities where few networks are present, a POP costs 1.25× to 1.5× where there is little or no carrier-neutral data center, and countries with thousands of networks, like Brazil and the US, bring more ISP customers. Big hubs such as Frankfurt, Amsterdam, New York and São Paulo keep their prices.
+- Every city now knows its country. Long-distance waves cost double only where they cross a border inside Africa, as they always meant to; a few northern routes, such as Kristiansand to Esbjerg and Anchorage to Halifax, lose a surcharge they picked up by mistake.

+
+- Attacks are more varied: sizes and lengths change from one attack to the next, and several can hit at once, each with its own controls in the NOC. Hosting game servers or cloud gaming makes attacks more frequent, as it does in real life (#153).

+- Attacks can now use Memcached amplification or an ACK flood. Flowspec catches the former; the latter need mitigation (#153).

+

+- The Networks list shows 100 networks at a time, with a button for the rest, so it opens quickly now that every country has its own networks.

+## Routing in a worker
+
+During play, each day's `compute()` runs off the main thread (`src/game/80-simulation/28-route-worker.js`), so a big
+network does not freeze the page once a day.
+
+- **Built from the page itself.** The worker is the page's own inline game script (`document.currentScript.textContent`)
+  run again from a Blob URL, after a short prelude of inert stand-ins for `document`, storage and the other DOM globals,
+  and the player's dictionary. Nothing is fetched: GitHub Pages still serves one page, and a release cannot mismatch.
+  In the worker `RW_IN` is true and `boot()` never runs; the catalogs are rebuilt by the same top-level code.
+- **The day split.** `dayTick()` is `dayPre()` (the world moves on), `compute()`, `dayPost()` (bills, moods, offers,
+  goals). In play, `frame()` calls `rwDay()` instead: `dayPre()`, then S and what routing reads of yesterday's R
+  (`R.load`, `R.l2route`, `R.efg`) are posted, and the next day waits until R comes back and `dayPost()` has run. So a day
+  sees exactly the routing it would have had in one go: same results, same random numbers. Half a day is never saved.
+- **What crosses.** `R.ef` and `R.fl` are lazy getters; their pieces (`R.efp`, `R.flc`) travel instead, typed arrays
+  transferred, and `efBuild()`/`flDefine()` (in `30-compute.js`) rebuild the same lazy R on the page.
+- **Actions mid-day.** Every `compute()` bumps `RW.gen`. If an action routed while a day was in flight, the worker's
+  answer is stale: it is dropped and the day ends with the action's R.
+- **Fallbacks.** Tests (`__TUBES_TEST__`, and jsdom has no Worker), `window.__TUBES_SYNC__`, a browser without workers, a
+  post that fails or a worker that errors take the synchronous path (`rwKill()` routes the day in flight on the page).
+- **Still on the main thread**, because the caller reads R right away: actions (`after()`), loading a game, failures and
+  events that fire during a day, standing orders, the chaos monkey, RouteScript what-ifs, the link panel's cut check and
+  automatic offers.

+## The weekly puzzle
+
+A puzzle week runs from Sunday 06:00 Berlin time to the next Sunday 06:00, and is named after the ISO week of
+its Monday (the week starting Sunday 1 November 2026 is `2026-W45`); `pzWeekKey()` and `pzWeekStart()` in
+`src/game/60-features/93-puzzles-weekly.js` handle summer time and the year boundary.
+
+Every Sunday `weekly-puzzle.yml` runs `scripts/weekly-puzzle.js`, which loads the real game headless, picks a
+theme the last three weeks did not have (region tour, ring, detour around a hub, ocean crossing, island hopping,
+latency sprint) and cities the last four weeks did not use, gives them traffic (content in the first city, eyeballs
+in the others, a circuit with a latency cap for a sprint), searches for the cheapest topology that connects them and
+the cheapest one that survives any single cut (a whole cable, or a trench), then sizes both with the game's own
+routing (`scripts/lib/puzzle-solver.js`: links and routers big enough for every flow, after any cut too, then as
+small as they go). The budget sits just above that N-1 build. Both references are judged by the game's own star
+code and must earn one and three stars, or the puzzle is thrown away. The file holds only ids, numbers and
+translation labels with their fill-ins
+(`{"v":2,"key","theme","cities","src","dem","via","avoid","budget","twist","name":{"l","p"},"joke":{"l","p"},"ref","rev"?}`).
+`--check` re-validates every file the way the game does.
+
+The game fetches `puzzles/weekly/<key>.json` (relative, same origin) only when the Puzzles list opens, and checks
+it field by field (`pzWkValid()`): known fields, playable cities, labels from the theme's own list, sane numbers.
+When it is missing, offline or wrong, the seeded weekly (`pzWeekly()`) stands in, so the weekly puzzle always
+works. The service worker fetches these files network-first and keeps a copy for offline play.
+
+The weekly ships without a release: the workflow commits only `site/puzzles/weekly/` to `main` (no version bump,
+so `auto-release.yml` stays quiet) and starts `release.yml` from the live release's tag with `weekly=true`, which
+rebuilds that exact release with every weekly file from `main` and deploys it. Every release build takes the
+weekly files from `main` too, so no deploy ever drops a published week.
+

+`site/scenarios/weekly/<key>.json`. A template (plain data in the script) picks a theme, a home city, rules from the

+# Series of Tubes as an MCP server
+
+`scripts/mcp.js` lets an AI client (Claude Code, Claude Desktop, any MCP client) play, inspect and debug the game
+through typed tools. It runs on your machine over stdio and loads the game from this checkout's `src/`, the way the
+tests do: one page in jsdom, seeded, with no animation loop. Nothing is hosted and the game page does not change, so
+it stays within [ADR 0001](adr/0001-github-pages-only.md): it is a local tool, like `npm run dev`.
+
+## Set it up
+
+```sh
+npm ci
+claude mcp add seriesoftubes -- node /path/to/seriesoftubes/scripts/mcp.js
+```
+
+Other clients take the same command (`node /path/to/seriesoftubes/scripts/mcp.js`) in their MCP server settings.
+`npm run mcp` starts it by hand; clients should use the `node` command, because `npm run` prints a line of its own first.
+
+A game is always loaded: a fresh On-call game in Frankfurt until you start or load another. Every game is seeded, so
+the same seed and the same moves give the same game.
+
+## Tools
+
+| Tool | What it does |
+|---|---|
+| `new_game` | Start a network in any home city with a preset (`freeze`, `oncall`, `bgp`, `sandbox`) and a seed |
+| `load_save`, `export_save` | Load an exported save (a path or JSON text, migrated as the game does) or write one the real game can import |
+| `status` | Date, cash, revenue and costs by kind, level, tier and why it is not Tier 1, the goal, traffic, reach, POPs, incidents |
+| `advance` | Run N days through `dayTick()`. Stops when a window needs an answer or the network goes bankrupt. Returns the log, new incidents, cash and the time each day took |
+| `network`, `city`, `find` | The world: policies and what a network asks for, its PoPs, cone and price; a city's exchanges, transit sellers, cables; search by name, id or ASN |
+| `traceroute` | The looking glass: which exit wins to a network and why, with the AS path |
+| `peering_check` | Would this network peer with you over a PNI or at an exchange, and the game's reason if not |
+| `hot_spots` | The fullest links, transit ports and PNIs, the transit bill by carrier, and the biggest traffic still on transit with the way off it |
+| `actions`, `act` | Every game action with its arguments, and running one as a button would |
+| `screen`, `panel`, `click`, `open_link` | The game's own windows and panels as text with numbered buttons; press one; open a link's build window |
+
+`act` and `click` run the same `ACT` actions the buttons dispatch, so the game's rules, prices and messages apply.
+They never reach files, save slots, settings, the title screen or the game speed (time moves only with `advance`).
+There is no tool that evaluates code in the page.
+
+## Looking into a bug report
+
+1. `load_save` with the save attached to the issue.
+2. `status` and `hot_spots` for the picture, `traceroute` and `peering_check` for one network's traffic.
+3. `advance` a few days and read `timing.slowestDays` for lag, or the log for what went wrong.
+
+## Code
+
+- `scripts/mcp.js`: the stdio transport (JSON-RPC 2.0, one message per line) and the protocol methods.
+- `scripts/lib/mcp-game.js`: the session (one game page) and the tool list with input schemas.
+- `scripts/lib/mcp-page.js`: runs inside the page and reads or drives the game through its own globals.
+- `tests/mcp.test.js`: the protocol, a game played through the tools, determinism, saves, and what stays out of reach.
+
+The tools read the game's internals (`S`, `R`, `ACT`, `NETS`…), which are not a stable API: a refactor in `src/` can
+break a tool, and `tests/mcp.test.js` is there to catch that in CI.
